pr_title: Prevent OS core dump creation for intentionally crashing tests
pr_body:
There are three coreclr tests that intentionally run a crashing secondary process. While the CreateDump invocation on crash for these tests was already disabled, the OS core dump creation was still happening. In the CI this was causing test machines getting out of disk space. This change disables OS core dump creation for those tests.

Close #113652

comments: @janvorli Can this be caused by your experiments that enable crash dumps for stack overflow tests in baseservices tests (#113533 and related PRs)?
I have not merged that PR in, but it is possible that just the CI running for the PR has caused it.

All the tests that crash a secondary process intentionally (unhandled exception, stack overflow, ...) end up generating dump via OS. They don't generate dumps via our CreateDump utility, as that's something that I have disabled in them a long time ago. 
I think we should be able to disable the OS generated dumps for the intentionally crashing processes by pinvoking `setrlimit` with `RLIMIT_CORE` set to 0.
I have it working locally, I will send out a PR soon.

FYI there are many instances of this where the helix machine never uploads any logs, see eg recent jitstress or outerloop runs (for instance: https://dev.azure.com/dnceng-public/public/_build/results?buildId=987437&view=ms.vss-test-web.build-test-results-tab)

Seems to also require azure linux 3?

review_comments: If I'm understanding this definition correctly, this will be invalid on 32-bit machines, right? I think we should consider making this a `CULong` instead. I'd like to make this not be a latent issue if we run these tests on a 32-bit non-Windows machine.
https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/setrlimit.2.html says that it is 64-bit value even on 32-bit systems, so the definition using `ulong` looks correct to me.

OpenBSD is defined as `int` - https://github.com/openbsd/src/blob/39200c1893dd71d26dd98a6230435389e2e9e665/gnu/gcc/gcc/sys-types.h#L131 . I see the linux kernel does define it as `__kernel_ulong_t`, which does appear to be `long long` on x86 - https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/5fc31936081919a8572a3d644f3fbb258038f337/include/uapi/linux/resource.h#L43-L46. Apple only defines it as 64-bit too, but I suppose that is because they only support 64-bit - https://developer.apple.com/documentation/kernel/rlim_t?changes=l__3__8.

Looks like `musl` as well - https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/include/sys/resource.h#n20

The referenced documentation does seem to also indicate that so I'm okay if we want to go with it.
We can enable this for Linux and macOS only (the only platforms where we actually need it).
